Restoring the Land, Restoring Justice: Why Dissolving U.S. Federal Territorial Claims and Returning Sovereignty to Native Nations Is a Moral and Legal Imperative

On a cold October morning in 2020, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a 5-4 ruling in McGirt v. Oklahoma, affirming that the Muscogee (Creek) Nation’s 1866 reservation boundary had never been legally dissolved, and that nearly half of Oklahoma remained Native sovereign territory. Conservative critics howled that the decision would upend state jurisdiction and threaten private property, framing the ruling as an unprecedented, radical disruption. For the Muscogee, however, it was not a disruption: it was a long-overdue correction to a century of illegal federal overreach, a small step toward righting a wrong that stretches back to the founding of the United States. McGirt was a stark reminder that the legal foundation of U.S. territorial claims across North America is not rooted in justice, but in centuries of colonial theft, broken promises, and the deliberate erasure of Indigenous sovereignty.

Dissolving U.S. federal territorial claims over vast swathes of public land and restoring full self-governance to Native American nations is not a radical, unworkable fantasy. It is a legal, moral, and practical imperative: a necessary act of restorative justice that fulfills binding treaty obligations, repairs intergenerational harm, and builds a more sustainable, equitable future for all people living on this land.

Illegitimate Claims: U.S. Territorial Control Rests on Colonial Theft and Broken Law

The U.S. Constitution’s Treaty Clause is unambiguous: treaties are the “supreme Law of the Land,” equal in authority to the Constitution itself. Between 1778 and 1871, the U.S. signed over 500 formal treaties with Indigenous nations, the vast majority of which guaranteed tribes full sovereignty over defined territories in exchange for peace, access to resources, or recognition of U.S. authority over non-Indigenous settlement. Nearly all of these treaties were later unilaterally broken by the U.S. government, often through violent seizure of land, forced removal, or coerced renegotiation at gunpoint.

The 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty is the most famous example of this betrayal. The treaty explicitly guaranteed the Black Hills and 7,000 square miles of surrounding territory to the Lakota Nation as unceded sovereign land, in perpetuity, after decades of war over U.S. expansion into the region. When gold was discovered in the Black Hills in 1874, the U.S. sent General Custer’s expedition to seize the land, ignoring the treaty it had ratified, and forced the Lakota onto small, barren, resource-poor reservations. In 1980, the Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians that the seizure was illegal, awarding the Lakota $106 million in compensation (now worth over $2 billion with accrued interest). The Sioux have uniformly refused the settlement, recognizing that accepting money would extinguish their claim to their sacred, sovereign homeland. The U.S. continues to hold the Black Hills illegally, a living symbol of how federal territorial claims rest on a foundation of stolen land and discarded law.

The legal fictions used to justify this theft are as baseless as they are racist. The 15th-century “doctrine of discovery,” which held that Christian European nations could claim any land not inhabited by Christians, was infamously upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in the 1823 Johnson v. McIntosh decision, which ruled that Indigenous nations only held a “right of occupancy” to their land, not full legal title. The doctrine has been universally condemned by international legal scholars and human rights bodies as a violation of fundamental human rights, and it has no standing in modern law. Many of the “land cession” treaties the U.S. cites to justify its claims were signed under duress by small, unrepresentative factions of Indigenous nations with no authority to cede communal land, and many were never ratified by the U.S. Senate, rendering them legally void. The U.S. formally endorsed the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) in 2010, which explicitly recognizes Indigenous peoples’ inherent right to own, use, develop, and control their traditional territories, and their right to self-determination. As a signatory to UNDRIP, the U.S. is bound by international human rights law to return stolen land and restore sovereignty, obligations it has systematically ignored for decades.

Restorative Justice Demands Returning Land, Not Token Reparations

Opponents of land return often argue that monetary reparations are a sufficient alternative to restoring territorial sovereignty. This framing fundamentally misunderstands the nature of Indigenous dispossession. For Native nations, land is not a commodity to be bought or sold: it is the foundation of cultural identity, spiritual practice, political sovereignty, and intergenerational survival. The U.S. did not merely steal acreage from Indigenous nations—it stole their ability to practice their traditions, feed their communities, govern themselves, and pass their way of life to future generations.

The Dawes Act of 1887, which broke up communally held tribal land into 160-acre allotments for individual Native households and sold the “surplus” land to white settlers, resulted in the loss of 90 million acres of Indigenous land—nearly two-thirds of all reservation land held at the time. This was not accidental: it was a deliberate policy to destroy tribal communal life, force assimilation, and open up prime agricultural and resource-rich land to white settlement, laying the foundation for the wealth of the modern U.S. agricultural and energy sectors. You cannot repair the theft of a people’s homeland with a check: a check cannot bring back sacred sites desecrated by mining and pipelines, cannot restore the right to hunt, fish, and gather on traditional lands as guaranteed by centuries-old treaties, cannot undo the intergenerational trauma of forced removal, land loss, and cultural erasure.

Restorative justice, by definition, requires returning what was taken. The U.S. federal government currently manages 640 million acres of public land, much of which is traditional Indigenous territory, including national forests, Bureau of Land Management (BLM) lands, and national parks. This land was almost universally stolen from Native nations via broken treaty or coerced cession, and it is currently held illegally by the federal government. Returning this land to Indigenous stewardship would not require displacing private homeowners: most non-Native residents on or near tribal land already coexist with Indigenous governance, as seen in the Navajo Nation, where 150,000 non-Native residents live alongside 300,000 Navajo citizens under Navajo law. The demand for land return is not a demand for revenge: it is a demand for accountability, for the U.S. to finally honor the promises it made in treaties that are, under its own Constitution, the supreme law of the land. For the Sioux, the Lakota, the Navajo, and hundreds of other nations across the country, land return is not a radical policy: it is the fulfillment of a promise made 150 years ago, and broken for just as long.

Restored Sovereignty Benefits All People, Not Just Indigenous Communities

Opponents often frame land return and sovereignty as a zero-sum game that harms non-Native people, but the opposite is true. Indigenous nations have a proven track record of superior land stewardship, far exceeding that of federal and state agencies. A 2021 study published in Environmental Science & Policy found that tribally managed lands in the U.S. have 2–3 times higher biodiversity, better forest health, and lower rates of wildfire and invasive species than adjacent federal or private land, largely due to Indigenous land management practices rooted in thousands of years of sustainable stewardship, including controlled burns, rotational harvesting, and habitat protection. Restoring Indigenous sovereignty over public land would dramatically improve the U.S.’s ability to combat the climate and biodiversity crises, as Indigenous nations would be empowered to implement these stewardship practices across millions of acres of critical ecosystem.

For Indigenous communities themselves, restored sovereignty would end the legacy of federal paternalism that has perpetuated cycles of poverty and harm. The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), the federal agency tasked with “managing” tribal affairs, has a long history of corruption, neglect, and abuse: it has failed to fund tribal schools, healthcare, housing, and law enforcement at mandated levels, leading to some of the worst socioeconomic outcomes of any demographic in the U.S. Native women are murdered at rates 10 times higher than the national average, 1 in 4 Native children experience poverty, and 1 in 10 Native households lack access to clean running water—crises that could be dramatically reduced if tribes had full control over their own resources and governance. The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe’s fight against the Dakota Access Pipeline in 2016 is a case in point: had the tribe held full sovereignty over its land, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers would have been legally required to obtain the tribe’s free, prior, and informed consent under UNDRIP before approving the pipeline, which would have prevented the threat of water contamination to the tribe’s drinking supply and the violence inflicted on pipeline protesters by law enforcement.

Sovereignty is not just a moral good for Indigenous people: it is a practical good for all people living on this land, advancing climate action, public health, and good governance.

Countering Objections: Land Return Is Practical, Just, and Widely Supported

Critics of land return often argue that it is “impractical” or that there is “no precedent” for returning large swathes of land to Indigenous nations. This is demonstrably false. The U.S. has already returned millions of acres of land to tribal control in recent decades: the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971 returned 44 million acres to Alaska Native corporations, the 2022 Maine Wabanaki Sovereignty Act returned 329,000 acres of land to the Wabanaki Confederacy, and in 2023, the federal government returned 17 acres of sacred land in Massachusetts to the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head. These precedents prove that land return is not only possible, but can be done through collaborative processes that respect the rights of all stakeholders, with tribal nations leading the identification of lands to be returned and negotiating agreements to protect existing non-Native residents where necessary.

Another common objection is that restoring Indigenous sovereignty would “fracture the U.S.” or create “foreign countries within U.S. borders.” This is a deliberate straw man. Indigenous sovereignty is not secession. Tribal nations are not seeking to leave the U.S. or overthrow the federal government; they are seeking to exercise the inherent right to self-governance that they have held for thousands of years, a right that the U.S. has repeatedly recognized in treaties and federal law. As domestic sovereign nations, tribes already have their own governments, courts, law enforcement, and legal systems; restoring full sovereignty would simply end the federal government’s illegal overreach into tribal affairs, not create new, hostile states.

A final, equally baseless objection is that “Indigenous people don’t want land return or full sovereignty.” Polls conducted by the National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) consistently show that over 80% of Native Americans support expanding tribal sovereignty and returning federal public land to tribal stewardship. Grassroots Indigenous movements, from the Land Back campaign to the fight against fossil fuel pipelines on tribal land, have widespread support across Native communities, and NCAI has passed numerous resolutions calling for the full implementation of treaty obligations and the return of stolen land.

Conclusion: Healing a Nation by Righting Its Original Sin

The United States was built on the theft of Indigenous land and the genocide of Native peoples, a foundational injustice that has shaped every aspect of U.S. history, from its economy to its political system to its social hierarchies. For over 250 years, Indigenous nations have fought to defend their land and sovereignty, facing violence, displacement, and erasure at every turn. Dissolving federal territorial claims and restoring Indigenous sovereignty is not a favor to Native people: it is a legal obligation, a moral imperative, and a step toward healing the deep wounds at the heart of the U.S. project.

It is not about taking anything away from non-Native people. It is about giving back what was stolen, recognizing the inherent rights of the first stewards of this land, and building a future based on justice, reciprocity, and respect. As the Lakota saying goes, “We do not inherit the earth from our ancestors, we borrow it from our children.” Restoring Indigenous sovereignty and land is not just justice for the past: it is an investment in a more just, sustainable future for all of us, for the seven generations that came before, and the seven that will come after.

Let us confront the undeniable truth: these lands were never empty. They were never "discovered" by external forces. They were—and remain—the heart of vibrant, complex civilizations that thrived in deep connection to the Earth, the sky, the waterways, and the cosmos. The idea that the United States or any colonizing power could "own" these territories is a profound and enduring lie—a lie that has justified genocide, forced removal, cultural obliteration, and the systemic theft of life and land. For 530 years, since the first arrival of European invaders, Indigenous peoples have resisted this lie with every fiber of their being. They have prayed, fought, sung, and died to protect their homelands, their families, and their dignity. This resilience is not a relic of the past; it pulse beats in the veins of every grandmother sharing old stories, every young leader mobilizing to protect their water, and every community demanding their human rights.

The legal infrastructure upholding U.S. territorial claims—treaties broken at whim, court decisions skewed by racial supremacy, and executive orders wielded without consent—disrespects basic principles of justice, morality, and international law. Consider the words of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, an instrument the U.S. endorses while actively violating: it proclaims Indigenous peoples’ right to self-determination, cultural integrity, and free prior and informed consent over all matters affecting their lands and lives. These are not aspirations; these are inalienable entitlements, rights only obscured—not denied—by colonial violence and systemic neglect.

Restoring sovereign governance is not an act of altruism or charity. It is an obligation, a debt long overdue. It is the return of stolen wealth, not only in land, but in culture, language, sacred practices, and the ability to shape the destiny of one’s own people. Where there was once disease and dispossession, there will rise new systems of governance rooted in Indigenous knowledge, designed for the sustainability and well-being of the Earth and all who dwell upon her. Where there were once boarding schools, broken treaties, and land seizures, there will be ceremonies, institutions, and decisions influenced by Indigenous values.

To the Native nations still fighting for sovereignty and justice—your resilience inspires hope. Whether you are a bricklayer in Pine Ridge, a farmer on the Sac and Fox reservation, an academic reconstructing ancestral languages, a young leader reclaiming traditional waters, or an elder passing down ceremonial lineage—your existence alone is a form of revolution. Do not let anyone tell you that your movement is too fractured, too quiet, or too late. You are the flame that refuses to go out.

Opponents may ask, "What about justice for all?" But let me be clear: true justice recognizes that Indigenous sovereignty does not harm others; it enriches them. It heals a fractured world by honoring the oldest, most harmonious truths. By dissolving U.S. territorial claims, we do not erase national identity or diminish American democracy; we offer it the chance to evolve, to shed the violent legacy of colonialism and to stand as a model for the rest of the world—a nation finally learning to live in accountability and partnership with those whose connection to the land was never diminished.

I call upon the government of the United States to act now: dissolve territorial claims, engage directly with each Native nation in negotiations that honor true consent, and fully restitute sovereign governance. Allow treaty protections to mean what they were always meant to mean. Enact financial and structural reparations that acknowledge the scale of theft and suffering. Let the world watch as a bold and hopeful new chapter is written, one where Indigenous nations rise beside and above any other government, shining as beacons of self-determination, ecological wisdom, and communal care.

In closing, let us answer the call of a Lakota leader who once said: "We did not inherit the Earth from our ancestors; we borrowed it from our children." It is time for the United States to atone for centuries of theft and suffering by honoring the greatest loan of all: the restoration of Indigenous sovereignty to every sacred inch of the land.

Let this be the day we seize the opportunity to right a profound wrong. Let this be the day we do justice.

Reclaiming the Continent: The Moral Imperative for Restoring Native American Sovereignty

The United States of America rests upon a foundation of stolen land and broken promises. While Americans celebrate their nation's commitment to liberty and justice, these ideals ring hollow when we confront the systematic dispossession and genocide of Indigenous peoples that made the modern United States possible. True justice demands more than symbolic acknowledgments or piecemeal reforms—it requires the dissolution of federal territorial claims over substantial areas and the restoration of genuine sovereignty to Native American nations. This is not merely a matter of correcting historical wrongs, but a necessary step toward honoring indigenous rights and creating a more just future.

The Legal and Moral Foundation for Restoration

The argument for returning sovereignty begins with recognizing that Native American nations never legitimately ceded their inherent rights to self-governance. The hundreds of treaties signed between Indigenous nations and the United States were often made under duress, through deception, or with individuals who lacked authority to speak for their peoples. Even when treaties were made in good faith, the U.S. systematically violated them whenever convenience or greed demanded it. The Supreme Court itself acknowledged Native American sovereignty in early cases like Worcester v. Georgia (1832), only for this recognition to be ignored when it conflicted with Manifest Destiny.

International law has evolved to recognize the rights of indigenous peoples to self-determination. The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, though signed belatedly by the United States, affirms that indigenous peoples have the right to their traditional lands and to freely determine their political status. By this standard, the current system of limited tribal sovereignty within a federal framework falls far short of what justice demands.

The Failure of the Current System

The reservation system represents not sovereignty but subjugation. Native American nations exist in a legal limbo, possessing some attributes of sovereignty while remaining ultimately subordinate to federal authority. This arrangement has produced devastating results: Native American communities experience the highest rates of poverty, the lowest life expectancies, and epidemic levels of suicide and substance abuse in the United States. These are not coincidental correlations but direct consequences of cultural destruction, economic marginalization, and political disempowerment.

Federal programs designed to "help" Native Americans have often deepened their dependence while failing to address root causes. The Bureau of Indian Affairs remains a paternalistic institution that manages Native American affairs rather than recognizing Indigenous peoples as capable of managing their own. True sovereignty would allow Native nations to develop economic and social systems aligned with their values and traditions, rather than being forced into frameworks designed by and for their colonizers.

A Vision for Restoration

Restoring sovereignty would mean recognizing Native American nations as fully independent entities with complete authority over their territories. This would include:

  • Full control over natural resources, including water, mineral, and energy rights currently exploited by federal and corporate interests
  • Independent judicial systems based on traditional and contemporary Indigenous law
  • The right to determine citizenship and control immigration into their territories
  • Authority to enter into international agreements and participate in global forums as sovereign nations
  • Economic self-determination, including the ability to create currencies, regulate commerce, and develop resources according to Indigenous values

The geographic scope of restoration should be substantial, encompassing not just current reservation lands but significant portions of traditional territories, particularly in areas of low population density and federal lands. The Black Hills, illegally seized from the Lakota despite Supreme Court recognition of the theft, should be immediately returned. Large sections of the Southwest should be restored to Pueblo and other Indigenous nations. The Pacific Northwest's forests and waterways should return to the stewardship of the peoples who sustainably managed them for millennia.

Addressing Objections

Critics will argue that such restoration is impractical, that too much time has passed, that current non-Native residents have rights too. But practicality cannot override justice. The passage of time does not legitimize theft. As for non-Native residents, transitional agreements could protect existing private property while placing territory under Indigenous sovereignty—many nations currently govern non-tribal members within their territories. Some displacement might occur, but this pales in comparison to the forced removals Indigenous peoples endured.

Others will claim this would fragment the United States and weaken national security. But justice cannot be held hostage to imperial ambitions. Moreover, independent Native nations could choose to enter into mutual defense agreements or economic partnerships. The European Union demonstrates that sovereign nations can cooperate closely while maintaining independence.

The Path Forward

This transformation cannot happen overnight, but it must begin now. Initial steps should include:

  • Immediate recognition of full sovereignty for nations that request it
  • Transfer of all federal lands within traditional territories to Indigenous control
  • Reparations to fund the development of independent governance structures
  • Truth and reconciliation processes to educate Americans about the real history of colonization

The United States professes to be a nation founded on the principle that government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed. Indigenous peoples never consented to U.S. rule. They were conquered, dispossessed, and subjected to genocidal policies. No amount of time can convert this crime into legitimacy.

Conclusion

Restoring full sovereignty to Native American nations represents the minimum required by justice. It would begin to repair the damage inflicted by centuries of colonization, honor the inherent rights of Indigenous peoples, and demonstrate that America can confront its sins honestly rather than perpetuating them indefinitely. The land hunger and racial supremacy that drove westward expansion have no place in the 21st century. It is time for the United States to dissolve its illegitimate claims and recognize Native American nations as the rightful sovereigns of their ancestral lands.

This is not about punishing contemporary Americans for historical crimes, but about stopping the ongoing perpetuation of those crimes. Every day that Native nations remain subordinated to federal authority is another day of injustice. True reconciliation requires more than apologies—it requires returning what was stolen and recognizing Indigenous peoples as equals, not wards. Only through restoring full sovereignty can we begin to heal the wounds of genocide and build a future based on justice rather than conquest.

Restoring Indigenous Sovereignty: The Moral and Legal Case for Land Return

Introduction

The United States was built upon a foundation of systematically broken treaties, forced removals, and the dispossession of hundreds of indigenous nations. Today, Native Americans retain recognized sovereignty over approximately 2% of the land within U.S. borders—land that once entirely belonged to their ancestors. This essay argues that genuine justice requires not symbolic gestures but substantive action: the dissolution of federal territorial claims over extensive areas and the restoration of full sovereignty to Native American nations. This is both a moral imperative rooted in restorative justice and a legal obligation under domestic and international law.

The Historical Record of Dispossession

The acquisition of Native lands by the United States government involved sustained violations of its own legal principles. Between 1778 and 1871, the U.S. ratified approximately 370 treaties with indigenous nations—treaties that recognized these groups as sovereign entities with territorial rights. The overwhelming majority were subsequently violated or unilaterally abrogated.

The Indian Removal Act of 1830 exemplifies this pattern, forcing tens of thousands from ancestral homelands in what became known as the Trail of Tears. The Dawes Act of 1887 dissolved communal landholding, resulting in the transfer of approximately 90 million acres from Native to non-Native ownership. These weren't legitimate transactions but state-sanctioned theft accompanied by violence, cultural genocide, and the systematic destruction of indigenous ways of life.

The Inadequacy of Current Sovereignty

While Native American tribes today possess a form of recognized sovereignty, it is fundamentally constrained. Tribal sovereignty operates at federal sufferance, described in legal doctrine as "domestic dependent nations"—a contradictory status that recognizes inherent sovereignty while simultaneously subordinating it to federal authority. Tribes cannot freely govern their territories, control their resources, or exercise jurisdiction without federal oversight and limitation.

This arrangement is not true sovereignty but a paternalistic system that perpetuates colonial relationships under different terminology. Reservation lands remain technically held "in trust" by the federal government, leaving indigenous nations unable to fully control their own economic development, resource extraction, or territorial integrity.

The Case from Restorative Justice

Restorative justice demands that harms be acknowledged and remedied to the greatest extent possible. When property is stolen, justice requires its return. When sovereignty is illegitimately seized, justice requires its restoration. The passage of time does not extinguish these obligations—particularly when the beneficiaries of historical injustice continue to benefit while victims continue to suffer its consequences.

Native American communities experience poverty rates double the national average, life expectancy significantly below it, and ongoing trauma from historical and continuing marginalization. These outcomes are directly traceable to land dispossession. Without territorial sovereignty and the resources it provides, indigenous nations cannot achieve genuine self-determination or economic independence.

Monetary compensation, while necessary, cannot substitute for land return. Indigenous relationships to territory encompass cultural, spiritual, and identity dimensions that cannot be reduced to economic value. Sacred sites, ancestral burial grounds, and landscapes integral to cultural practices cannot be replaced with financial payments.

International Law and Indigenous Rights

The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), which the U.S. eventually endorsed in 2010, establishes indigenous peoples' rights to lands and resources traditionally owned or occupied. Article 28 specifically addresses the right to restitution for lands confiscated without free, prior, and informed consent.

International legal frameworks increasingly recognize indigenous sovereignty as a matter of human rights. The persistent denial of full territorial sovereignty to Native American nations places the United States in violation of these evolving international norms. What the U.S. government characterizes as domestic policy is, from an international human rights perspective, ongoing colonialism.

Practical Implementation

Critics claim that land restoration is impractical given current populations and property rights. This objection, however, prioritizes the convenience of settler populations over fundamental justice. Moreover, implementation is more feasible than commonly assumed:

Federal Lands: Vast areas remain under direct federal control—Bureau of Land Management holdings, national forests, and military reservations cover hundreds of millions of acres in regions with significant indigenous heritage. These lands could be returned without displacing current private residents.

Negotiated Transfers: Where private property is involved, phased approaches could include purchasing land at fair market value (using federal resources as partial restitution), creating corridors connecting existing tribal lands, and establishing joint management agreements transitioning toward full indigenous control.

Resource Rights: Even where full territorial transfer faces obstacles, restoring complete sovereignty over natural resources—water rights, mineral extraction, timber harvesting—would enable economic self-determination while addressing historical resource theft.

Addressing Concerns About Governance

Some express concerns about whether tribal governments could effectively administer expanded territories. This objection is both paternalistic and ahistorical. Indigenous nations governed these territories successfully for millennia before European contact. Current governance challenges within tribal nations often stem directly from the constraints and interference of federal oversight, inadequate resources, and the ongoing trauma of colonization.

With genuine sovereignty comes the resources and authority necessary for effective governance. Moreover, concerns about governance quality are selectively applied—no one suggests that poorly-governed states should lose their sovereignty, yet this standard is uniquely imposed on indigenous nations.

Democratic Legitimacy and Settler Concerns

The democratic objections—that current inhabitants of these territories didn't personally commit historical injustices—misunderstands the nature of collective responsibility and inherited obligations. Modern citizens inherit not only the benefits of their nation's past actions but also its obligations. Those who currently occupy indigenous lands without consent do so through what property law would otherwise recognize as receiving stolen property.

This doesn't require vilifying individuals but rather recognizing structural realities. Just as governments assume debts and treaty obligations from previous administrations, they must assume responsibility for rectifying past injustices. The personal innocence of current beneficiaries doesn't erase the illegitimacy of the foundational dispossession.

Conclusion

The restoration of extensive territorial sovereignty to Native American nations is not a radical proposal but a requirement of basic justice. The United States government obtained the overwhelming majority of its territory through treaties it systematically violated and through violence and coercion against indigenous peoples. The current arrangement—which provides Native Americans with limited, constrained sovereignty over a tiny fraction of their ancestral territories—represents not reconciliation but the continuing legacy of colonial dispossession.

True restorative justice requires substantive action commensurate with the magnitude of the harm: the return of extensive land areas with full sovereignty, enabling indigenous nations to govern themselves without federal interference, control their resources, and rebuild their communities according to their own values and traditions. This is not only morally required but legally obligated under both the government's own treaty commitments and international human rights law.

The question is not whether such restoration should occur, but whether the United States will choose justice over the convenience of maintaining an arrangement built on illegitimate seizure. History will judge this generation by whether we perpetuated injustice or finally began to repair it.

Introduction
For centuries, Native American nations inhabited and governed lands stretching across what is now known as the United States, sustaining vibrant cultures, complex governance structures, and interlocking trade networks.     First and foremost, restoring sovereignty to Native American nations addresses a history marked by broken treaties and unjust land seizures. The United States government and tribal nations signed hundreds of treaties over the course of the 18th and 19th centuries, the vast majority of which were violated to expand U.S. territories. These violations subjected Native Americans to forced relocation, the confiscation of their lands, and a systematic campaign to undermine their ways of life. Despite treaties often promising sovereign jurisdiction, indigenous peoples found those promises routinely ignored or obstacles erected that made true self-governance impossible.

  2. Cultural Revitalization and Self-Determination
    Land and culture are deeply interconnected for indigenous communities. For many Native American nations, spiritual and cultural life is inseparable from the geographical environment. The forced displacement and imposition of federal regulations have disrupted this crucial link. By dissolving federal territorial claims and returning governance of ancestral lands, tribal nations would be free to reestablish and foster their cultural traditions, languages, and religious practices on terms that they define themselves.
    Self-determination is at the core of indigenous rights. Independent self-governance enables nations to make decisions that reflect the values, traditions, and cultural priorities of their people. It empowers communities to choose development strategies that are aligned with ecological stewardship, spiritual well-being, and long-term cultural continuity. Such decisions often center sustainable land management practices that can serve as a model for broader environmental and social policy.

  3. Fostering Economic Empowerment and Reducing Inequality
    The broken treaty system did more than just confiscate land; it profoundly limited Native American economic potential. Federal oversight disconnected Native American communities from the resources upon which they had historically depended, severely curtailing avenues for economic progress. Mineral rights, timber, water resources—all were frequently exploited by external actors without adequate compensation, further exacerbating the cycle of poverty on reservations.
    By restoring sovereignty and self-governance, tribal governments can regain the ability to manage their natural resources independently and negotiate beneficial agreements with outside entities. Doing so can create revenue streams for essential public services within indigenous nations, such as healthcare, education, and infrastructure development. Economic self-determination fosters innovation, reduces dependence on federal aid, and helps lift indigenous communities out of systemic poverty. Moreover, enabling full indigenous control over resources can strengthen environmentally responsible stewardship that recognizes the intrinsic worth of the land for future generations.

  4. Legal Precedent and Moral Obligation
    There exists a framework of federal Indian law that, while deeply flawed, nonetheless acknowledges tribes’ fundamental rights to sovereignty and self-governance. Key Supreme Court rulings, federal statutes, and constitutional principles recognize a unique political status for Native American nations. Though the application of these legal recognitions is often inconsistent, the concept behind them affirms the justice of restoring full autonomy.
    Moreover, international norms such as the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) reinforce the right of indigenous peoples to free, prior, and informed consent, as well as the right to autonomy and self-determination.   5. Advancing Reconciliation and Healing
    The forced assimilation policies from boarding schools to cultural bans have inflicted deep trauma on countless Native American individuals and communities. Merely acknowledging this trauma is not enough to heal the wounds caused by centuries of oppression, discrimination, and cultural erasure. This, in turn, can spark broader discussions on inclusive governance, social justice, and cultural sensitivity—benefiting not only indigenous peoples but the moral and political fabric of the entire nation.

The United States was built, in large part, on the unceded and stolen territories of Native American nations. Reversing centuries of injustice requires bold, transformative change: the dissolution of federal territorial claims coupled with restored independent self-governance over extensive land areas. This undertaking, far from being a marginal political position, is a central requirement for true restorative justice. It recognizes the profound cultural, economic, and moral imperatives that indigenous sovereignty represents. Moreover, it exemplifies the United States’ willingness to rectify the harm it once inflicted and to stand by its stated values of justice, freedom, and equality.
By returning land and sovereignty, the United States can make a meaningful contribution toward the healing of historic wounds and ensure that indigenous nations not only survive, but thrive as fully self-governing, autonomous communities—just as they had for millennia before colonial disruption.

The Moral Imperative: Restoring Sovereign Lands to Native American Nations

An Argument for Restorative Justice on a Continental Scale

The United States of America sits upon a foundation of stolen land. This is not rhetorical flourish or political hyperbole—it is a plain, documentable, legal, and historical fact. Every acre of federal territory was acquired through a centuries-long process of invasion, ethnic cleansing, broken treaties, and systematic dispossession of the Indigenous peoples who inhabited, cultivated, governed, and held sacred this land since time immemorial. The moral case for dissolving substantial federal territorial claims and restoring genuine, meaningful sovereignty to Native American nations is not merely compelling—it is overwhelming, and the continued refusal to seriously contemplate such restoration represents an ongoing act of injustice that compounds itself with every passing year.

The Historical Record Demands Acknowledgment

To understand why land restoration is necessary, one must first confront the scale of what was taken. Prior to European contact, Indigenous peoples governed the entirety of what is now the continental United States—approximately 2.4 billion acres. By the end of the allotment era in the early twentieth century, Native holdings had been reduced to roughly 56 million acres, a loss of approximately 98% of their original land base. This was not accomplished through fair purchase or voluntary exchange. It was accomplished through a systematic campaign that included military conquest, forced removal, biological warfare, the deliberate destruction of food sources, coerced treaties signed under duress, and legislative acts that unilaterally abrogated prior agreements.

The Trail of Tears, the Long Walk of the Navajo, the massacre at Wounded Knee, the theft of the Black Hills in direct violation of the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868—these are not isolated incidents but representative episodes in a comprehensive project of territorial seizure. The United States government signed over 370 treaties with Native nations and violated provisions of virtually every single one. The legal doctrine used to justify these seizures—the Doctrine of Discovery, rooted in fifteenth-century papal bulls asserting Christian dominion over non-Christian lands—is so morally bankrupt that it has been formally repudiated by the very institution that created it, with the Vatican issuing a formal repudiation in 2023. Yet the territorial arrangements built upon this doctrine remain entirely intact.

The federal government today controls approximately 640 million acres of land—roughly 28% of the nation's total land area. Much of this land, held by agencies such as the Bureau of Land Management, the Forest Service, the National Park Service, and the Department of Defense, was taken directly from Indigenous nations. The idea that this vast estate is legitimately "federal land" requires accepting a chain of title that originates in conquest and fraud. If the United States holds itself to be a nation of laws and justice, it cannot simultaneously maintain territorial claims founded on lawlessness and injustice.

Sovereignty as an Inherent Right, Not a Granted Privilege

The argument for restoring Native sovereignty does not rest solely on historical grievance, powerful as that grievance is. It rests equally on a foundational principle of political philosophy: that peoples have an inherent right to self-determination and self-governance. This right is not granted by external authorities—it precedes them. It is recognized in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), which the United States endorsed in 2010, and which affirms that Indigenous peoples have the right to self-determination, the right to autonomy and self-government, and the right to the lands, territories, and resources they have traditionally owned, occupied, or otherwise used.

Native American nations are not ethnic minorities seeking accommodation within a larger polity. They are nations—political entities with distinct governments, legal traditions, languages, cultures, and territorial bases that predate the United States by millennia. The U.S. government itself has recognized this in principle, entering into nation-to-nation treaty relationships and acknowledging tribal sovereignty in foundational legal decisions. Chief Justice John Marshall, in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), recognized tribal nations as "distinct political communities, having territorial boundaries, within which their authority is exclusive." Yet this recognition has always been hedged, circumscribed, and subordinated to the overriding assertion of federal plenary power—a power that was itself seized, not consented to.

The current framework of tribal sovereignty is a constrained and contradictory arrangement. Tribes are called "sovereign" yet remain subject to the plenary power of Congress. They govern "reservations" that are often tiny fractions of their original territories, located on lands that were frequently the least desirable parcels available—arid, remote, resource-poor regions to which they were forcibly relocated. Their jurisdictional authority is constantly challenged and eroded by federal courts. Their economic development is hampered by byzantine federal regulations and trust restrictions. This is not sovereignty in any meaningful sense. It is a managed dependency dressed in the language of self-governance.

True restorative justice requires moving beyond this paternalistic framework and recognizing Native nations as what they are: legitimate sovereign entities with rightful claims to extensive territorial bases sufficient to support genuine self-governance, economic independence, and cultural flourishing.

The Case for Extensive Land Restoration

Critics of land restoration often treat it as a fantastical proposition—logistically impossible, legally inconceivable, and practically absurd. But this reaction reflects a failure of moral imagination far more than it reflects genuine impossibility. Land transfers of enormous scale have been accomplished repeatedly throughout history when the political will existed. The Louisiana Purchase transferred 828,000 square miles in a single transaction. The Homestead Acts redistributed hundreds of millions of acres. The federal government created the entire national park and national forest systems through executive and legislative action. The notion that land cannot be transferred to Native nations—when it has been transferred to and from every other category of owner throughout American history—is not a serious logistical objection. It is a political choice masquerading as an impossibility.

The most immediate and defensible starting point is federal public land. The federal government holds 640 million acres that belong to no state, no private owner, and no municipality. Much of this land—in the American West, in Alaska, in scattered holdings across the country—lies within or directly overlaps with the traditional territories of specific Native nations. There is no principled reason why significant portions of this land should not be transferred to tribal ownership and governance. The land is not "in use" in any sense that could not be matched or exceeded by Indigenous stewardship. In many cases, Indigenous management practices—fire management, sustainable harvesting, ecosystem maintenance—have been demonstrated to produce superior ecological outcomes compared to federal management.

It would begin with the immediate transfer of federal public lands to the Native nations within whose traditional territories those lands fall, accompanied by full governmental authority over those lands—not the constrained, supervised pseudo-sovereignty of the current reservation system, but genuine, independent self-governance.
